Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-24
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Redwood CSM), Tom Garcia (Aegis Head of ML), Rina Kapoor (Aegis Infra), David Lee (Aegis CTO)
---
Summary: Weekly POC sync to review Redwood's benchmark runs vs the customer's baseline provider. Discussed latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput (qps), batching, quantization tradeoffs, KV cache effects, and next steps to reproduce and validate numbers. Some minor transcription errors (product names, acronyms) present.
---
Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll kick off, quick roll call?
[00:08] Tom Garcia: hey Tom here, rina, david on my side.
[00:12] Rina Kapoor: hey all, got my notes up.
[00:15] Maya Chen: cool, so last week we ran the baseline comparison runs, we have fresh numbers, liam are you able to go over the bench sheet?
[00:24] Liam O'Connor: yeah sure, i'll pull up the sheet, um quick caveat first, some of the logs from the baseline provider were truncated so we normalized as best we could, there may be a small skew in tail latencies.
[00:37] David Lee: ok that's expected - we told them to limit retention so not surprising.
[00:40] Liam O'Connor: alright, looking at the p50/p95/p99 for the 8k-token clinical summarization workload on the 13B model variant: Redwood hosted (opt-quant) p50 = 65ms, p95 = 210ms, p99 = 420ms. Baseline provider reported p50 = 110ms, p95 = 380ms, p99 = 780ms. Throughput at steady state: Redwood ~85 qps for our configured batch of 8 with continuous batching, baseline ~50 qps.
[01:05] Tom Garcia: wow 85 qps is better than we expected, can you confirm same artifacts used (same prompt sets, same seq len distribution)?
[01:13] Liam O'Connor: yes we used the shared prompt set - the sheet link is in the notes. There was a small difference: baseline used FP16 single-GPU instances with an older kernel, we used quantized INT8 path with our kernel selection. That gives lower token cost and lower latency in our runs.
[01:30] Rina Kapoor: there might be concern about quality - did you check decoding differences or model output drift because of quant?
[01:36] Maya Chen: good call, we ran the rouge/bleu style checks and spot human inspection on 200 samples, differences were negligible for the clinical summarization prompts, we included the eval tab in the sheet.
[01:46] Tom Garcia: what's the unit cost delta? we need cost/per-1000-tokens to compare economics.
[01:51] Liam O'Connor: on our hosted plan numbers, cost per 1k tokens for this workload is roughly $0.42 vs baseline provider's $0.73 given their higher tail latency and lower batching efficiency. Numbers in sheet, but ballpark.
[02:05] David Lee: baseline provider had a wider p99 tail, we care about tail for our latency SLOs, are those absolute numbers or do they include network variance?
[02:13] Liam O'Connor: they include end-to-end measured latencies from client to response. For fairness we removed client-side synthetic jitter but included network hop times; baseline logs were captured from their edge so slight differences. We also ran an isolated internal test (both on same vpc peering sim) where Redwood p99 tightened to ~360ms.
[02:30] Rina Kapoor: did you test with KV cache warm vs cold?
[02:33] Liam O'Connor: yes - warm cache gives a big improvement on repeating prefixes. With a warm KV cache p95 dropped to 140ms and p99 to 300ms for the same model and batch config. That's in the cache tab.
[02:45] Tom Garcia: can you explain the batching tradeoffs? our requests are bursty but many are short, is continuous batching hurting small tail latency?
[02:53] Liam O'Connor: good question, continuous batching helps throughput by aggregating small requests; for bursts of short queries we configured max batch size 8 and a latency cap of 20ms before dispatch so we balance latency. For strictly single-req latency we can reduce batch window which lowers qps; we showed a tradeoff curve in the sheet.
[03:12] Maya Chen: just to interject, for the PoC our recommendation was to tune per-route: critical low-latency endpoints use smaller batch window and dedicated instances, high-throughput non-latency-sensitive endpoints use larger batches.
[03:25] Rina Kapoor: what's the Dedicated vs Hosted delta if we reserve capacity? any different performance profile?
[03:30] Liam O'Connor: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools; latency is slightly more predictable under sustained load because you avoid noisy neighbors and we can pin kernels. In our tests dedicated-ish setup moved p99 down about 10-15% compared to shared hosted, but cost model is different.
[03:44] David Lee: security question - for dedicated or private we need KMS integration and audit logs, any blockers?
[03:50] Maya Chen: no blockers - Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM and audit trails, we can share the SOC2/ISO packet. I'll add that to next steps.
[03:58] Tom Garcia: there were a couple of outlier runs where baseline's throughput temporarily spiked higher, can we look at concurrency and autoscale behavior?
[04:06] Liam O'Connor: yep, those were likely bursting tests on their side; their autoscaler climbs slower under cold start. Our autoscale config for the PoC is more aggressive, which kept steady throughput. We can simulate cold-starts if you want.
[04:20] Rina Kapoor: can you also share the exact instance types and kernel versions used?
[04:23] Liam O'Connor: sure - Redwood runs used Ampere X2A-40g equivalent, kernel v2.6.3 optimized; baseline used older A100 stack with CUDA 12.1 but older kernel. I'll add exact SKUs to the sheet.
[04:36] Tom Garcia: one of our internal stakeholders flagged hallucination risk with quantization - any notes?
[04:41] Maya Chen: we did targeted QA on hallucination-sensitive prompts; no meaningful difference but we'll run a larger eval suite if you want.
[04:47] David Lee: what's the plan to make the benchmark reproducible on our side? we need to run the same harness; can you share the harness and container?
[04:55] Liam O'Connor: yes, we can provide the benchmarking harness repo link and a docker image. We'll also share the script we used to normalize timestamps and compute p95/p99.
[05:04] Tom Garcia: perfect. for the next run, please include per-request trace ids so we can correlate with our logs.
[05:10] Liam O'Connor: noted. we'll include trace ids.
[05:13] Maya Chen: ok to recap real quick - redwood will: 1) share updated benchmark sheet with p95/p99 breakdown and dedicated-run numbers (Maya) 2) share harness + docker image + kernel/sku details (Liam) 3) send SOC2/ISO and KMS integration docs (Priya). Aegis will: 1) send baseline provider raw logs and sample traces (Tom) 2) validate eval outputs on their side and flag quality deltas (Rina).
[05:36] Rina Kapoor: timeline - we can validate and push results in 48 hours for the sample set.
[05:40] Maya Chen: great, so next sync after those artifacts land, probably friday next week?
[05:44] Tom Garcia: friday works.
[05:46] David Lee: quick question on pricing - if we hit predicted 85 qps steady state, can we get an estimate for committed reserved capacity?
[05:54] Maya Chen: yeah we'll model committed tiers and give a monthly estimate; i'll include a couple of commit scenarios in the sheet.
[06:02] Tom Garcia: thanks team.
[06:04] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with artifacts.
[06:08] (meeting ends)
